references.text: The previous context describes how Gideon divided his 300 men and gave them trumpets and jars with torches inside, as preparation for the attack described in verse 19.
The immediate continuation tells of the result of the attack: all three groups blew their trumpets, broke the jars, and the Lord turned the enemy's swords against each other.
At the morning watch, the Lord looked down on the Egyptian camp from the pillar of fire and cloud, creating confusion among them—a similar divine intervention at night watch as in Gideon's attack.
The use of trumpets (shofar) as a military signal is prescribed in the Mosaic Law to gather the people for battle.
At the fall of Jericho, the Israelites blew trumpets as a sign of God's intervention in battle, similar to the use of the shofar in Gideon's night attack.
Saul also divided his people into three groups and attacked at the morning watch, a military strategy resembling Gideon's approach.
Abimelech used the same tactic of dividing his men into groups and attacking at dawn, which recalls Gideon's strategy.
